bp: A short-video app is always choosing one next video from an enormous supply, and the choice is better when the system understands more than the last few swipes. A viewer may have old interests that return, habits that repeat at certain times, or long arcs of curiosity that only become visible after thousands of watched videos. Douyin therefore wants recommendation models that can read very long user histories, up to 10,000 past actions, while still answering fast enough for a production feed. The paper serves the practical problem of remembering more without making the service too slow or expensive. Its title captures the pressure: make the remembered history long, but keep the serving path fast. The work is not only about prediction quality. It is about whether an end-to-end learned recommender can use long histories at billion-scale traffic under real latency, storage, communication, and compute budgets.
wh: The difficulty comes from the shape of the comparison. A common sequence model asks every past event to compare with every other past event, so it can learn which parts of the history matter together. That is manageable for short records, but with 10,000 videos the number of pairwise comparisons grows explosively. Douyin cannot spend production time and memory building a full map of how all old videos relate to one another whenever it needs to score a new target. At the same time, simply cutting the history short throws away useful evidence. In short-video recommendation, a user can reveal interests over a long span, and the abstract reports predictable gains as history length and model capacity grow. The hard part is therefore a three-way tension: keep old preference evidence, train the system end to end, and still respect the tight response-time and cost budgets of full-traffic deployment.
naive: A smart beginner might keep the standard long-sequence machinery and feed all 10,000 watched videos into it. The model would then let every history item inspect every other history item, hoping to build a rich description of the user's taste. That fails because the cost grows with the square of the history length, so the price of adding more memory rises much faster than the memory itself. Another beginner response is to keep only a recent window, such as the last few hundred or few thousand videos. That is cheap, but it makes the system forget older signals that may still explain the current recommendation. A third shortcut is to precompute a user summary, but then the model may no longer learn the whole recommendation path end to end.
ap: The central move is to stop asking the history to fully talk to itself. For a recommendation decision, the immediate question is not every relationship among all old videos. It is whether a candidate target video can find useful evidence inside the user's history. Stacked Target-to-History Cross Attention, or STCA, makes that narrower question explicit: the target points into the history and gathers relevant signals from it, in stacked layers, instead of building all history-to-history comparisons. The paper then attacks duplicated work at the request level. When the same user request contains several targets to score, Request Level Batching shares the user-side encoding across those targets rather than rebuilding it repeatedly. Finally, length-extrapolative training trains on shorter windows and serves on longer ones, so the model learns the mechanism cheaply but applies it to 10,000-history inference.
mech: The input is a user's ordered history of watched or interacted short videos and a set of target videos that the recommender may need to score for the current request. First, the system represents the target and the historical videos in a form the model can compare. The key comparison is directed: instead of letting each history item compare against all other history items, the target asks which historical positions are useful for judging this target. STCA repeats this target-to-history lookup through stacked layers, so the target can gather evidence from the long record without paying for a full history self-comparison map. Because the cost grows roughly in proportion to the history length, adding more past videos is far less punishing than a quadratic design. Next, Request Level Batching groups multiple targets from the same user request. The long user history is encoded once and reused across those targets, which lowers storage, communication, and compute while keeping the learning objective unchanged. During training, the model sees shorter history windows, which saves training cost. During serving, the same learned operation is applied to much longer histories, up to 10,000. The output is a set of target scores or ranked choices that can be used inside Douyin's production recommendation feed.
math: The main mathematical idea is selective weighting under a resource budget. Attention, in plain terms, means giving different pieces of evidence different voting strength before combining them. In this paper the votes come from historical videos, and the question is how much each one should shape the score for a target video. Full self-attention over the history builds a table of all history-item pairs; that table has quadratic cost, meaning doubling the history makes the pair table about four times larger. STCA changes the object being built. It builds target-to-history comparisons, so the number of comparisons grows linearly with history length for each target path. The sequence idea is also central: the history is not just a pile of videos, because order and long-range repeated behavior can matter for the next recommendation. Request Level Batching uses another simple mathematical economy: reuse a shared computation when several later scores depend on the same user-side information. Length extrapolation assumes the learned comparison rule is not tied only to the exact training length. The tradeoff is accuracy versus cost: remember more history, but use a comparison structure whose price does not explode.
dots: This paper connects recommendation, ranking, sequence modeling, attention, and efficiency. Like other recommender-system work in the repo, it is about sorting a huge pile so a user sees a small useful set. Its distinctive pressure is production scale: the recommender is not allowed to become slow just because the user history is informative. It also fits the sequence concept, because the useful evidence is an ordered record of past actions rather than a static profile. It fits the attention concept because the model must decide which old videos should count more for the present target. It neighbors efficiency-and-scalability papers because its contribution is partly architectural and partly systems-oriented: reduce wasted comparisons, share computation within a request, and train under a cheaper length while serving a longer one. Compared with recommendation papers about fairness, explanations, or multimodal item content, this one asks how much memory a deployed feed can practically afford.
ww: The approach should work better than the naive choices because it matches the actual decision. A target video does not need a complete social map among all 10,000 historical videos before it can ask whether the user is likely to engage. It needs enough targeted evidence from the history: similar interests, recurring patterns, or older actions that still help this candidate. By making the target query the history, STCA keeps the part of attention that selects relevant evidence while removing many comparisons that do not directly serve the current score. Request Level Batching works for a different reason: in one user request, the long user record is common to many candidate targets, so recomputing it separately is waste. Sharing that encoding saves resources without changing what the model is trying to learn. Length-extrapolative training works if the learned lookup behavior transfers from shorter to longer histories. The abstract's reported monotonic gains as history length and model capacity grow support the idea that extra history is adding useful signal rather than only noise.
po: The payoff is a production path for using 10,000-length histories in a short-video recommender without abandoning latency and cost constraints. The abstract says the system enables efficient end-to-end training, lowers sequence-related storage, communication, and compute through request-level sharing, and generalizes to much longer histories at inference without extra training cost. It also reports predictable gains from scaling history length and model capacity, and deployment at full Douyin traffic with significant improvements on key engagement metrics while meeting production latency. In practical terms, the feed can remember more of a user's behavior and still respond fast enough to be usable.
limits: The claims depend on several assumptions. The user history must contain useful long-range evidence; if older actions are mostly stale or misleading, longer memory may add cost without better recommendations. The length-extrapolative strategy assumes rules learned on shorter windows still behave sensibly on 10,000-item histories. The abstract does not fully specify which engagement metrics improved, by how much, or how the method behaves for cold-start users with little history. It also does not prove that target-to-history comparison captures every interaction that full history self-comparison would capture. The result is strongest for a large production short-video setting like Douyin, where repeated requests per user and massive traffic make shared computation especially valuable.
